passage:
Monday: Gurleen's first week at the Berlin office. Her team lead, Siddharth, raised a problem with her report bluntly in the meeting. She went home feeling humiliated and cried on the phone to her mother.

Thursday: Over coffee, Siddharth, who had grown up in Delhi and worked in Germany for six years, explained that here people often said problems directly and it wasn't personal. "It took me a year," he admitted. Gurleen wasn't sure she believed him.

Three weeks later: A German colleague, Jonas, told her flatly her slides were confusing. Gurleen breathed, said thanks, and asked which slide. He showed her, then added, "The data is very good." She noticed she didn't need him to soften it. She also noticed she still preferred to be gentle herself, and that was fine.

qa.q: Who explained that direct feedback wasn't personal?
qa.a: Siddharth, her team lead, explained it over coffee.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel after the first meeting, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt humiliated; she cried on the phone to her mother that evening.

qa.q: What helped Gurleen adapt over those weeks?
qa.a: Understanding the local style from someone who had adjusted himself, and practising asking specific questions instead of taking it personally.

qa.q: How might Jonas see Gurleen's response to his feedback?
qa.a: He likely saw her as open and professional, since she thanked him and asked which slide.

grounding: Shows a young professional adapting to a direct communication style abroad while keeping her own gentler manner.

passage: Sit down, Gurleen puttar, I'll tell you about Dubai. I was twenty when I went to work at the port. My supervisor was Filipino, my roommate Egyptian, the canteen man from Kerala. First month, I shook hands with a colleague's wife before she offered her hand. She stepped back. I felt like a fool. My Egyptian roommate explained, kindly, that many people there waited for the woman to offer first. I didn't know. So I learned: watch first, ask when unsure, and don't assume your home rules are the only rules. And I learned people forgive mistakes if you're respectful. My Filipino boss once came to our gurdwara for langar. He covered his head without being told. That's respect. Remember it when you go to Canada.

qa.q: Where was the narrator's supervisor from?
qa.a: The narrator's supervisor was Filipino.

qa.q: How did the narrator feel after the handshake moment?
qa.a: The narrator felt foolish and embarrassed at making a colleague's wife uncomfortable.

qa.q: What advice from the narrator could Gurleen use in Canada?
qa.a: Watch first, ask when unsure, and don't assume home customs are the only way.

qa.q: How might the Filipino boss have felt covering his head at the gurdwara?
qa.a: He probably wanted to show respect for a custom that wasn't his, and it clearly meant a lot to the narrator.

grounding: Shows an elder passing on lessons about respecting different social norms while working among many cultures.

passage: Kavitha had two hours to prepare the Bengaluru office for a video call with a new client team in Nairobi, and the conference room's internet kept dropping. Her senior, Trisha, was stuck in traffic. Kavitha had planned to open with the numbers, the way her team liked. But last week one of the Kenyan managers had spent five minutes asking about everyone's families before business. So she rewrote her opening: a warm welcome, a question about how their week had gone, then the plan. When the connection finally held, the Kenyan lead smiled and talked about his daughter's school exams. Trisha joined late, heard the relaxed tone, and messaged Kavitha: 'Nice start 👏'. They got through every agenda point anyway, just ten minutes later than planned.

qa.q: Where was the client team calling from?
qa.a: The client team was calling from Nairobi.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha change her opening?
qa.a: She remembered the Kenyan manager's warm small talk last week and wanted the client to feel respected in their own style.

qa.q: What worked about Kavitha's approach under pressure?
qa.a: She adapted quickly to the client's norms while still covering every agenda point, balancing warmth with work.

qa.q: What would change if Kavitha had started straight with numbers?
qa.a: The Kenyan team might have found it abrupt and felt less comfortable, which could have made the new relationship harder.

grounding: Shows a young professional adapting her communication style to another culture's norms under time pressure.

passage: In her first week at a design studio in Coimbatore, Ira kept waiting for Pema, her new teammate from Thimphu, to say whether he liked her logo drafts. He only said, 'Hmm, this one is also interesting,' and smiled. Ira, used to her old Delhi office where people said 'no, redo it' bluntly, assumed he approved. She sent the draft to the client. The next day Pema quietly showed her his own notes: three concerns he had hoped she would notice. Ira felt her face heat. That evening, over chai, she asked him how feedback worked where he grew up. 'We don't like to embarrass someone,' he said. 'But I should have been clearer.' They agreed he would write one clear concern per draft, and she would ask directly, 'What would you change?' By Friday Ira found she admired how gently he said hard things.

qa.q: Where is Pema from?
qa.a: Thimphu.

qa.q: Why did Ira's face heat when Pema showed his notes?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, realising she had read his polite 'interesting' as approval and sent the draft too soon.

qa.q: What agreement helped them work across their styles?
qa.a: Pema writes one clear concern per draft and Ira asks directly what he would change, bridging indirect and blunt habits.

qa.q: How might Pema have felt when Ira sent the draft to the client?
qa.a: Perhaps uneasy and partly responsible, since he admits he should have been clearer.

grounding: Shows two colleagues from different backgrounds adapting their feedback styles and coming to respect each other.

passage:
'Bhaiya, why do you keep saying sorry to the auto driver?' Kishore asked, dropping onto the sofa.
Ujjwal laughed. 'Habit. A year in Osaka does that.'
Papa looked up from the paper. 'And you came home at exactly seven like a train. Suddenly punctual?'
'There, if a meeting says ten, people are there before ten. My first week I strolled in at ten-fifteen, and my team lead didn't say anything, just looked at the clock. I wanted to disappear.'
'So they're strict,' Kishore said.
'Not strict exactly. Just different. People are very quiet on trains, nobody talks loudly on the phone. I learned by watching before I spoke.'
'And did you teach them anything?'
Ujjwal grinned. 'A colleague now makes chai with ginger. Badly. But he tries.'
Papa smiled. 'Good. You went respectfully and came back the same boy.'

qa.q: Where did Ujjwal spend a year?
qa.a: In Osaka.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when his team lead looked at the clock?
qa.a: Deeply embarrassed; he says he wanted to disappear.

qa.q: What approach helped Ujjwal adapt in Osaka?
qa.a: Watching before speaking, noticing norms like punctuality and quiet trains, and adjusting without judging them as strict.

qa.q: How does Papa see the change in Ujjwal?
qa.a: He is pleased that Ujjwal adapted respectfully while still coming home as the same boy 😊

grounding: A family conversation shows a young man describing how he adapted to different work and social norms abroad.

passage: When I, Nazia, moved from Lucknow to a Chennai office, I thought I was polite. At home we wrap everything in "if it's not too much trouble" and "whenever you get a chance". In my first month I asked my colleague Ankita, whenever she got a chance, for a file I needed that afternoon. She took me at my word and sent it three days later. I was quietly furious. Then in a review my team lead said my updates were "too long to find the point". I went home and cried into my curd rice. It took a chat with Ankita, who had moved from Kolkata two years before, to see it. "Here people say what they need, plainly. It's not rude. It's respect for time." So I tried. "I need this by four." It felt harsh in my mouth. Nobody minded. And when Ankita heard I missed Lucknow's long greetings, she started saying "Adaab" every morning, badly.

qa.q: When did Ankita send the file?
qa.a: Three days later.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when the file came three days late?
qa.a: Nazia felt quietly furious, not yet realising the polite phrase had signalled there was no hurry.

qa.q: What change did Nazia make, and why did it work?
qa.a: Stating needs plainly, like 'I need this by four', which matched the office's way of respecting time.

qa.q: How might Ankita have seen Nazia's first requests?
qa.a: Ankita took the polite wording literally, so she likely thought there was no rush and was surprised to learn otherwise.

grounding: A young professional moving between Indian regions adapts from indirect to direct requests, and a colleague honours her customs.

passage: Supervisor's note, week 6, Tarun (intern, client team). This week Tarun joined his first call with our German client. He arrived three minutes late with a friendly apology and a long warm-up about the weather. The client's lead cut in politely: "Shall we start?" Tarun looked flustered for the rest of the call. Afterwards Gargi, who has worked with this client for two years, took him aside and explained that for this team, starting on time and getting to the point is the courtesy; the warmth comes later, over lunch or at the end. Tarun listened, then asked good questions about how they give feedback. On Thursday's call he joined two minutes early, opened with the agenda, and saved a short friendly line for the close. The client's lead thanked him by name. I will pair him with Gargi on the next project. — Ms Kulkarni

qa.q: How late was Tarun to the first call?
qa.a: Three minutes late.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling after the client's lead cut in?
qa.a: Tarun felt flustered and embarrassed for the rest of the call.

qa.q: What did Gargi explain, and how did Tarun apply it?
qa.a: That for this client, punctuality and getting to the point are the courtesy; Tarun joined early, opened with the agenda and kept friendliness for the close.

qa.q: How might the client's lead have seen Tarun on Thursday?
qa.a: The lead likely saw a respectful, prepared colleague and appreciated the change, thanking him by name.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows an intern adapting his communication style to a client's different work norms.

passage:
Thursday night
Week three of the Dubai internship, and it's Ramadan. I hadn't thought it through. On Monday I brought parathas and ate them at my desk right next to Yusuf, who's fasting. He said nothing, just smiled. Later Rhea from HR quietly mentioned that the pantry is where people usually eat during these weeks. My ears went hot. I'd been rude without knowing.
I apologised to Yusuf at five. He laughed. "You're fine. But now you owe me: iftar, Thursday."
So tonight I went. His mother fed me like I hadn't eaten in a year. They asked about langar, and I explained how everyone sits on the floor and eats the same food. Yusuf's dad said, "Same idea as the iftar tents. Feed whoever comes."
Next week I'm bringing Mummy's pinni for the office. After sunset.
— Amandeep

qa.q: Where does Rhea say people usually eat during these weeks?
qa.a: In the pantry.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when Rhea mentioned the pantry?
qa.a: Amandeep felt embarrassed, ears hot, realising the desk lunch had been inconsiderate without meaning to be.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do after learning the norm?
qa.a: Apologised to Yusuf, accepted the iftar invitation, and planned to share sweets after sunset, respecting the custom.

qa.q: How does Yusuf see Amandeep's mistake?
qa.a: Yusuf isn't offended; he laughs it off and turns it into an invitation, which suggests warmth and patience.

grounding: A young intern abroad learns a workplace norm during Ramadan, apologises, and shares customs with a colleague's family.

passage:
Sachin, from Mumbai, had been posted to a bank branch in a small town in Nagaland. On his first day, he spoke fast Hindi and ordered people around the way he did in the city.
The staff went quiet. Noor, a local colleague, took him aside at lunch.
"Here, we greet everyone properly first, even if it takes time. And we don't raise our voice."
Sachin felt his face heat. "I didn't mean to be rude."
"I know. That's why I'm telling you."
The next day, he greeted each staff member by name, asked about their families, and learned a few words of Nagamese. At the end of the week, the peon brought him local tea.
"Welcome," he said. Sachin felt, for the first time, part of the place.

qa.q: Where was Sachin posted?
qa.a: To a bank branch in a small town in Nagaland.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when his face heated?
qa.a: Sachin felt embarrassed, realising he'd seemed rude without meaning to.

qa.q: What changes did Sachin make to adapt to the local norms?
qa.a: Greeting everyone properly, asking about families, speaking gently and learning a few words of Nagamese.

qa.q: How might Noor see Sachin's changes?
qa.a: Noor likely feels respected and glad her advice was taken well.

grounding: A young banker adapts his communication to work respectfully in a new cultural setting.

passage:
In Berlin, Tuan joined a design studio. On day one, his colleague Noa said bluntly, "This layout doesn't work. The text is too small."
Tuan felt hurt. In Vietnam, his old boss would have said it more gently, over coffee.
He avoided Noa for two days. Then she came over. "Did I upset you?"
"A little. Where I'm from, feedback is softer."
Noa nodded. "Here, directness means respect. I say it straight because I think you can fix it. But I can say what I like first."
Tuan smiled. "And I'll try not to take it personally."
The next week, Noa said, "Colours are great. Text is still too small." Tuan laughed. "Fair."

qa.q: What did Noa say was too small?
qa.a: The text.

qa.q: What was Tuan feeling after Noa's first feedback?
qa.a: Tuan felt hurt and avoided Noa for two days.

qa.q: What did Tuan and Noa each do that helped?
qa.a: Noa asked if she'd upset him and adjusted; Tuan explained his norms and agreed not to take directness personally.

qa.q: How does Noa see direct feedback?
qa.a: Noa sees it as a sign of respect, trusting the person can fix it.

grounding: A young designer adapts to direct feedback norms in a new country, with mutual understanding.

passage:
In his first month as an intern at the Pune office of a German engineering firm, Vijay kept waiting to be told what to do. In meetings he nodded at everything. When his supervisor, Klaus, said, "This design is wrong, the tolerances are too loose," Vijay felt humiliated. In his old college, a teacher would never say it so bluntly in front of others.
Alka, a senior engineer who'd worked there five years, found him in the pantry. "He's not insulting you. That's how they talk here. Direct. He'd be confused if you just nodded."
"So I should argue?"
"Not argue. Say what you think, clearly. Ask when you don't know."
In the next meeting, Vijay said, "I chose these tolerances because of cost. Would tighter ones be worth it?" Klaus looked surprised, then pleased. They discussed it for ten minutes.

qa.q: What did Klaus say about Vijay's design?
qa.a: "This design is wrong, the tolerances are too loose."

qa.q: How did Vijay feel when Klaus criticised the design in front of others?
qa.a: Vijay felt humiliated, since at his old college a teacher would never be so blunt in public.

qa.q: What adjustment helped Vijay work well across cultures?
qa.a: Speaking up clearly with his reasons and asking questions, instead of silently nodding, fitted the direct style of the office.

qa.q: How might Klaus have seen Vijay's silent nodding in the first month?
qa.a: Klaus may have been confused, not knowing whether Vijay agreed or understood, since he expects people to speak up.

grounding: Shows a young intern adapting his communication to a direct workplace culture with a colleague's help.

passage:
Dear Saurabh,
Three weeks into my internship in Osaka, and I'm learning more about manners than about engineering.
On day one I said "hi" to my manager and started talking about my project. Everyone went quiet. Later my buddy explained: introductions here are formal, with a bow, and you wait for the senior person to lead. I felt so embarrassed.
Other things: nobody leaves before the manager on some days; meetings are for agreeing on what's already been discussed in small groups before; "that might be difficult" often means no.
I'm trying not to judge it or pretend I'm Japanese. I watch, I ask my buddy, and I say sorry when I get it wrong. People have been kind about my mistakes.
Next weekend, they're taking me to a festival. I've been practising my bow in the mirror.
Madhuri

qa.q: What can "that might be difficult" often mean, according to Madhuri?
qa.a: It often means no.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel after the day-one mistake?
qa.a: Madhuri felt embarrassed after the room went quiet.

qa.q: What is Madhuri doing well in adapting to a different work culture?
qa.a: Madhuri watches, asks the buddy and apologises for mistakes, respecting local norms without pretending to be someone else.

qa.q: How might Madhuri's Japanese colleagues see these efforts?
qa.a: They probably appreciate the respect and effort, which is why they're kind about mistakes and invited Madhuri to the festival.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult adapting communication and respecting different workplace norms abroad.

passage:
Amandeep, you asked what moving from Delhi to Chennai for work was like. I'm Swati, and the first month I was a disaster.
I spoke loudly, joked with seniors, called everyone "yaar". At lunch, I made a face at curd rice. My team was polite, but I could feel them pulling back.
Then my colleague Revathi invited me home for Pongal. Her grandmother served me on a banana leaf and waited to see if I'd eat with my hand. I did, badly. Everyone laughed, kindly.
On the way back I realised I'd been expecting Chennai to adjust to me. So I changed. I learned basic Tamil greetings. I stopped joking with seniors until I knew them. I asked about things instead of making faces.
Now my team teases me for liking curd rice more than they do. And I say "vanakkam" to the watchman every morning.

qa.q: What did Swati's colleague Revathi send an invitation for?
qa.a: Pongal, at Revathi's home.

qa.q: How did Swati feel when the team pulled back?
qa.a: Swati felt uncomfortable and a bit lonely, sensing that behaviour from Delhi wasn't landing well.

qa.q: What changes helped Swati fit in without losing Swati's own identity?
qa.a: Learning Tamil greetings, reading the room with seniors, and asking with curiosity instead of judging the food.

qa.q: How might Revathi's grandmother have felt watching Swati eat with her hand?
qa.a: Revathi's grandmother probably felt amused and warmed that the guest tried their way of eating.

grounding: Shows a young adult adapting communication and social behaviour after moving to a different cultural region for work.

passage: Kishore here. I shared a desk row with Dilnaz during her first months at our Seoul office, so I saw it up close. In week one she said "No, that won't work" in a meeting, the way we'd say it back in Hyderabad, and the room went very quiet. Our team lead just smiled tightly. After that, I noticed she watched more than she talked. She started sending her objections in writing before meetings, framed as questions: "Could we check the timeline together?" She handed over documents with both hands, the way our lead did. At team dinners she waited for the eldest to start eating. But she didn't vanish either. When a plan really was wrong, she still said so, just earlier and more gently. By spring the lead was asking her opinion first. I can't say what she felt inside, but she looked more at home.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz start sending before meetings?
qa.a: She sent her objections in writing, framed as questions.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz have felt after the quiet meeting in week one?
qa.a: She probably felt embarrassed and unsure of herself, since afterward she watched more than she talked.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz's adjustments get right?
qa.a: She changed how she disagreed, in writing, earlier and gently, and respected local customs, while still speaking up when a plan was wrong.

qa.q: How does the team lead's view of Dilnaz change?
qa.a: The lead moves from a tight smile after her blunt no to asking her opinion first by spring, which shows growing respect.

grounding: A colleague observes a young professional adapting her communication to a new work culture without losing her voice.
